text: Over the past month or so,
I think many people have been concerned about
the war between the U.S., Israel, and Iran —
a conflict that has shaken the global situation.
Today I'd like to start with this topic,
but from a different angle.
I think war serves as a kind of stage —
one where you can see how astonishing human invention can be.
In this war, you see all kinds of different weapons.
I don't know if you've been following the news,
but in the upper-left corner here, that's the MOAB —
the Mother of All Bombs.

This Mother of All Bombs
is the strongest in the conventional category.

you have to step into unconventional weapons —
nuclear weapons, for example.

underground nuclear facilities.

is a torpedo —
a Mk 48 heavyweight torpedo.

Someone once said: every weapon humans have invented
has eventually been deployed on a battlefield.
And in fact, throughout the history of war,
weapons have gone through several —
three major revolutions, you could say.
Let me walk through them as a kind of framework.
If someone asked you, in all of history,
which was the greatest empire?
You might say the Mongol Empire — and you'd be right.
Because across the vast expanse of Eurasia,
the Mongol Empire stretched across an enormous swath of the continent.
Why were they so formidable?
The Mongols' greatest strength was their cavalry.
I think in this painting —
when I found this image,
I felt that the person who painted it
really understood the Mongol cavalry.
Why?
Because one of the Mongols' deadliest assets was their bow —
the famous recurve bow.
See how both ends curve outward?
Compared with bows of the 13th century,
it was three or four times more powerful.
At close range it could pierce armor.
The other thing was the stirrup.
The foothold you step into when mounting — the stirrup.
The Mongols didn't invent the stirrup,
but they pushed its use to the limit.
Why? Because of the stirrup,
the rider could stand on his horse,
and shoot arrows in a full 360 degrees,
dominating his opponent. Combined with that powerful bow,
they had a famous tactic called the Parthian shot —
the moment you thought they were retreating and chased them,
they'd turn around and put an arrow in you.
That's why in the 13th century
the Mongols swept across everything — no one could stand against them.
So what was the first weapons revolution?
It was gunpowder — applying gunpowder to military use.
That gave us firearms, and also artillery.
So if someone asks you which was the largest empire,
by sheer area, it wasn't the Mongols.
By area — and you know this one well —
it was the empire on which the sun never set: the British Empire.
In history,
by total area, the British Empire was the largest.
That was the first revolution
in warfare and in weapons.

a technical term.

If the U.S. ever came under nuclear attack,
these are the response options on the table.
Rare, medium-rare, or well done?

So if you're hit by a nuclear strike,
what's the response? Mutually assured destruction?
Or some other kind of reply?

was the invention of the nuclear bomb.
After the nuclear bomb was invented,
it wasn't long before two were dropped on Japan.
And America has remained extremely powerful — even today.

What the aircraft sees,

what he sees is exactly what

on the Ukrainian battlefield,

A single soldier, a single individual,

he can also simultaneously control aerial drones.
So there's surveillance — like the earlier example:
he spots the Russian soldiers,
then can dispatch a bomb-carrying vehicle
to take out the enemy.
You can see this is coordinated combat —
letting a single soldier control
unmanned weapons across sea, land, and air.

has been developing on the battlefield,
making the effectiveness even more formidable —
the effectiveness of using robots. Why?
Because AI can take massive amounts of sensor data —
huge volumes of data — and digest and analyze it,
assess the battlefield situation,
and then offer options for action.

You may have heard of one called

This weapon is very unusual. Why?
A normal missile, once launched, flies forward.
But this one flies upward.
It punches out to the edge of the atmosphere,
the edge of space.
Why does it do that?
First, there's less drag at the edge of space —
so it has much longer range.
When it comes back down to ground level,
re-entering the atmosphere,
it dives so fast
that interception becomes very difficult.
Understand?
There's actually another reason.
Because look — this is day one of the war,
the early stage of the conflict.

So they chose this weapon for exactly that reason.

The principle is that simple:
you emit signals outward,
they bounce off something and come back,

It scans 360 degrees, right?
But most radars have a blind spot.
That blind spot is the zenith —
directly overhead.
You rarely see a radar sweeping straight up.
Understand?
So this Blue Sparrow's special feature is:
it comes in right at the zenith —
straight down on top of you.
So why on day one?

an electronic jamming system.

you can't control it anymore.

fiber-optic cables —
